rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī derives dassāhā from the doubled root d-s-s and tadīs, meaning to conceal one thing within another, with one s changed to yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهو إخفاء الشيء في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He supports the morphology by comparing other forms whose original doubled consonants were simplified, including taqaḍḍaḍa, labibt, and mulabbab.
rows.anchor: أصل تقضى البازي تقضض البازي

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites say the righteous make themselves visible, while the sinful hide; generous Arabs advertise their lodgings and fires, unlike misers who conceal their whereabouts.
rows.anchor: أما المعتزلة فذكروا وجوها توافق قولهم

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: One Muʿtazilite explanation is that the loser inserts himself among the righteous despite not belonging to them.
rows.anchor: أي دس نفسه في جملة الصالحين وليس منهم

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the person immerses himself in sins.
rows.anchor: في المعاصي حتى انغمس فيها

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Another explanation is that persistent sin and company with sinners plant wickedness in a person's soul.
rows.anchor: وذلك بسبب مواظبته عليها ومجالسته مع أهلها

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Another explanation is that neglecting obedience for sins makes a person obscure, forsaken, and forgotten, like something concealed.
rows.anchor: فصار كالشيء المدسوس في الاختفاء والخمول

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Rāzī's own school says the soul has failed and lost when God misguides it, makes it wicked, nullifies it, and destroys it.
rows.anchor: نفس أضلها الله تعالى وأغواها وأفجرها

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says the oath by God's noblest creatures establishes the success of the purified and loss of the forsaken, so people do not suppose they purify or ruin themselves independently of prior decree.
rows.anchor: الواحدي رحمه الله : فكأنه سبحانه أقسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Talazzā means to catch fire, blaze, and glow; the verb is used of a fire blazing, and Jahannam is called Laẓā from it.
rows.anchor: تلظى أي تتوقد وتتلهب وتتوهج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reads seeking the Lord's face as an exception from a different category than the favor or benefit owed to the giver, like saying there is nobody in the house except a donkey.
rows.anchor: مستثنى من غير جنسه وهو النعمة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ offers an alternative ellipsis: understand that the spending is only for seeking God's face, as in 2:272.
rows.anchor: وذكر الفراء فيه وجها آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pious giver is not repaying a prior gift or favor, which would merely discharge a debt; reward is earned by giving because God commanded and urged it.
rows.anchor: لأن ذلك يجري مجرى أداء الدين

rows.speaker: المجسمة
rows.claim: The anthropomorphists appeal to the word face in the verse.
rows.anchor: المجسمة تمسكوا بلفظة الوجه

rows.speaker: الملحدة
rows.claim: The atheists appeal to the phrase his Lord the Most High as though it entailed another lord.
rows.anchor: الملحدة تمسكوا بلفظة { ربه الأعلى }

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني
rows.claim: In al-Imāma, al-Bāqillānī assigns the feeding-for-God verses to ʿAlī and this verse to Abū Bakr; both acted for God, but ʿAlī also feared Judgment, so Abū Bakr's station is higher.
rows.anchor: ذكر القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني في كتاب

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: One view says seeking God means seeking His essence, which is impossible, so the phrase must mean seeking His reward and honor.
rows.anchor: من الناس من قال : ابتغاء الله بمعنى

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: Another view sees no need for an ellipsis; the underlying dispute is whether a servant can love God's essence or only His reward and honor, discussed under 2:165.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من قال : لا حاجة إلى هذا الإضمار

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb reads ibtighāʾ in the nominative, following a dialect that makes the exception nominative after a negative; the cited verse line illustrates the usage.
rows.anchor: يحيى بن وثاب : { إلا ابتغاء وجه ربه } بالرفع

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والمبرد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Mubarrad derive the word from farewell at parting; the light reading means He did not leave you, while tawdīʿ intensifies the act of leaving.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة والمبرد : ودعك من التوديع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qilā means hatred; qalahu yaqlihi is used of hating someone.
rows.anchor: بالغ في تركك والقلى البغض

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ understands the clause as wa-mā qalāka, with the object pronoun omitted.
rows.anchor: الفراء : يريد وما قلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for omitting the second kāf is that the first kāf in waddaʿaka already supplies it.
rows.anchor: حذفت الكاف اكتفاء بالكاف الأولى في ودعك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted kāf also preserves the sūra's verse endings in yāʾ.
rows.anchor: ولأن رؤس الآيات بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unexpressed object can make the denial broad: God did not hate the Prophet's companions or anyone he loved through the Resurrection, affirming that one is with whom one loves.
rows.anchor: فائدة الإطلاق أنه ما قلاك ولا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes report that Gabriel's arrival was delayed, so the polytheists said God had abandoned and hated the Prophet; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: المفسرون : أبطأ جبريل على النبي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the delay lasted forty nights; the Prophet complained to Khadīja, who suggested that his Lord might have forgotten or hated him.
rows.anchor: السدي : أبطأ عليه أربعين ليلة

rows.speaker: أم جميل
rows.claim: Umm Jamīl, Abū Lahab's wife, taunted the Prophet that his satan seemed to have left him.
rows.anchor: إن أم جميل امرأة أبي لهب قالت له

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports that after revelation paused, the Prophet told Khadīja that his Lord had left and hated him; she denied this and said God began his honor to complete it.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن أنه قال

rows.speaker: الأصوليون
rows.claim: The theologians of legal principles reject the report of the Prophet thinking God had left him, since he knew removing him from prophecy would violate divine wisdom and revelation's timing follows benefit.
rows.anchor: وطعن الأصوليون في هذه الرواية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the report about the Prophet's complaint is sound, Rāzī says it can mean he was testing Khadīja to reveal her understanding, or letting people recognize it.
rows.anchor: ثم إن صح ذلك يحمل على أنه كان مقصوده عليه الصلاة والسلام أن يجربها ليعرف قدر علمها

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj gives the period without revelation as twelve days.
rows.anchor: ابن جريج : اثنا عشر يوما

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī gives the period without revelation as fifteen days.
rows.anchor: الكلبي : خمسة عشر يوما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās gives the period without revelation as twenty-five days.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس : خمسة وعشرون يوما

rows.speaker: السدي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and Muqātil give the period without revelation as forty days.
rows.anchor: السدي ومقاتل : أربعون يوما

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes say the pause followed the Prophet's promise to answer the Jews about the Spirit, Dhū al-Qarnayn, and the Companions of the Cave without saying “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: فذكر أكثر المفسرين أن اليهود سألت رسول الله

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says a puppy kept at home for al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn caused the delay; Gabriel explained that angels do not enter a house containing a dog or image.
rows.anchor: ابن زيد : السبب فيه كون جرو في بيته

rows.speaker: جندب بن سفيان
rows.claim: Jundub ibn Sufyān says a stone struck the Prophet's finger; he recited a couplet about a bleeding finger in God's path, after which revelation paused.
rows.anchor: جندب بن سفيان : رمى النبي عليه الصلاة بحجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed report mentions someone among them who did not trim his nails, in the discussion of the revelation pause.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان فيهم من لا يقلم الأظفار وههنا سؤالان

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet told Gabriel he had missed him, and Gabriel replied that he longed even more but was commanded, citing 19:64.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال لجبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delay need show only that the Prophet missed what was preferable, not that he was hated; a person who misses the best is not thereby detested.
rows.anchor: أقصى ما في الباب أن ذلك كان تركا للأفضل والأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assuring a beloved person that he is not hated would be odd without cause, but it honors him when enemies have spread that charge and he is distressed by it.
rows.anchor: إذا ألقوا في الألسنة أن السلطان يبغضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation's pause demonstrates that the Qurʾān comes from God: if it originated with the Prophet, it would not have been withheld from him.
rows.anchor: هذه الواقعة تدل على أن القرآن من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One connection to the preceding verse is that a revelation pause could signal not dismissal but death; death is better because the Prophet's state with God in the Hereafter surpasses his worldly state.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المعنى أن انقطاع الوحي لا يجوز أن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another connection is that after God honored him by denying abandonment, He assures him that his Hereafter standing will be greater still.
rows.anchor: حصل له بهذا تشريف عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī's own proposed reading takes ākhira and ūlā as later and earlier conditions: God will increase the Prophet in honor and rank day by day.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يكون المعنى وللأحوال الآتية خير لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reason the Hereafter is better is that worldly life lets the Prophet do what he wants, while in the Hereafter God does what He wants for him.
rows.anchor: إنك في الدنيا على خير لأنك تفعل فيها ما تريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet will be reunited with his community in Paradise; the community is like his children, and the Qurʾān calls wives their mothers and asks for spouses and offspring as comfort to the eyes.
rows.anchor: يجتمع عندك أمتك إذ الأمة له كالأولاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter is better because it is the Prophet's earned possession, whereas this world is not his; even a lesser owned good would be preferable to what is not owned.
rows.anchor: الآخرة خير لك لأنك اشتريتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this world disbelievers attack the Prophet, whereas in the Hereafter his community witnesses for nations, he witnesses for prophets, and God witnesses for him.
rows.anchor: الآخرة خير لك من الأولى لأن في الدنيا الكفار يطعنون فيك أما في الآخرة فأجعل أمتك شهداء على الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly benefits are few, mixed, and temporary, while the Hereafter's pleasures are abundant, pure, and lasting.
rows.anchor: أن خيرات الدنيا قليلة مشوبة منقطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording addresses the Prophet alone because some of his companions would fare badly in the Hereafter; universalizing the promise would be false, while naming only the obedient would expose sinners and hypocrites.
rows.anchor: من كانت الآخرة شرا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī contrasts Moses's assurance that God is with him with Muhammad's assurance that God is with “us,” since Muhammad's companions there were only the Prophet and Abū Bakr, both destined for happiness.
rows.anchor: وأما محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم فالذي كان معه لما كان من أهل السعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report about Moses says a drought prayer with thousands failed for three days because a talebearer was among them; after God said the talebearer had died, Moses found seventy funeral biers at the prayer place.
rows.anchor: وروي أن موسى عليه السلام خرج للاستسقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story illustrates God's concealment even of enemies; the saying “if not for elders bowing” hints that this community is favored, since one sinner once held back thousands, while one obedient person brings mercy to sinners.
rows.anchor: فهذا ستره على أعدائه فكيف على أوليائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise specifies how far the Hereafter's superiority reaches: God's gift will extend to the limit of what the Prophet wishes and accepts.
rows.anchor: لم يبين أن ذلك التفاوت إلى أي حد يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also answers why the Hereafter is better: God will give the Prophet everything he wants, beyond what worldly life can contain.
rows.anchor: فقيل ولم قلت إن الأمر كذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the promised benefit as a thousand palaces of white pearl in Paradise, with musk soil and everything appropriate to them.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس : ألف قصر في الجنة من لؤلؤ أبيض

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب وابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the promised honor as the Prophet's intercession for his community.
rows.anchor: المروي عن علي بن أبي طالب عليه السلام وابن عباس

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet said he would not be satisfied while even one person from his community remained in the Fire.
rows.anchor: يروى أنه عليه السلام لما نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the promise must include intercession for sinners, since the Prophet was commanded to seek forgiveness for believers and would want that request answered, not refused.
rows.anchor: تعالى أمره في الدنيا بالاستغفار فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intercession reading best fits the preceding assurance: God will not be angry with the Prophet's companions and followers, thereby pleasing and comforting him.
rows.anchor: كأنه تعالى يقول لا أودعك ولا أبغضك بل لا أغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many intercession reports say the Prophet is satisfied by pardon for sinners; together with the promise to give him what pleases him, they establish intercession.
rows.anchor: الأحاديث الكثيرة الواردة في الشفاعة دالة على أن رضا الرسول

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says his grandfather's satisfaction is that no monotheist enter the Fire.
rows.anchor: عن جعفر الصادق عليه السلام أنه قال

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Bāqir says the Prophet's satisfaction means intercession for people who profess God's oneness until he declares himself satisfied; he calls this the most hopeful verse for the Prophet's family, unlike the Qurʾān readers' choice of 39:53.
rows.anchor: الباقر ،   أهل القرآن يقولون : أرجى آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the promise concerns worldly benefits, it includes victory at Badr and the conquest of Mecca, mass conversion, victories over Qurayẓa and Naḍīr, campaigns across Arabia, later caliphal conquests, Persian treasure, and Islam's spread and prestige.
rows.anchor: أما لو حملنا هذا الوعد على أحوال الدنيا فهو إشارة إلى ما أعطاه الله تعالى من الظفر بأعدائه يوم بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers a comprehensive reading that includes the good of both worldly life and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: الأولى حمل الآية على خيرات الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular promise addresses the Prophet because he is the aim and his community follows him.
rows.anchor: أحدها ) أنه المقصود وهم أتباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honoring the Prophet's companions honors him, since he rejoices more in their reward than in his own; unlike other prophets' “myself, myself,” he says “my community, my community.”
rows.anchor: أني إذا أكرمت أصحابك فذاك في الحقيقة إكرام لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet endured bodily injury and prayed for guidance when his face was wounded, but treated interference with prayer as injury to religion; Rāzī contrasts his refusing takfīr for long-term prayer abandonment or obstruction with takfīr for harming even a hair or sandal piece.
rows.anchor: وحين شغلوك يوم الخندق عن الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The use of sawfa indicates that the Prophet's death was not near and that he would live for some time after this promise.
rows.anchor: أنه يدل على أنه ما قرب أجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future wording answers the polytheists' claim that Muhammad would die, as the preceding wording answered their claim that God had abandoned him.
rows.anchor: فالله تعالى رد عليهم بعين تلك اللفظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says Gabriel speaks to the Prophet throughout this sūra because Gabriel longed for him and his speech, and God made Gabriel address him with these glad tidings.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة من أولها إلى آخرها كلام جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The author of al-Kashshāf parses the lām as an emphatic lām of inception; an omitted subject is understood, yielding “and you will surely be given,” since a lām of oath would require emphatic nūn.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب «الكشاف » : هي لام الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combining the emphatic lām with the delayed future particle assures that the gift will certainly come, with its delay serving a wise purpose.
rows.anchor: أن العطاء كائن لا محالة ، وإن تأخر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says the clause coordinates with the meaning of “Did We not expand,” understood as “We have expanded,” rather than its surface wording; literal coordination would require “and We will remove.”
rows.anchor: قال المبرد : هذا محمول على معنى ألم نشرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wizr means the weight of sin; Rāzī links the phrase to 6:31, where people carry their burdens, and to the forgiveness promised in 48:2.
rows.anchor: معنى الوزر ثقل الذنب ، وقد

rows.speaker: علماء اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists explain that a back under a heavy load makes a faint naqīḍ sound, like loaded litters, ribs, or an overloaded camel; this pictures the burden on the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال علماء اللغة : الأصل فيه أن الظهر

rows.speaker: أصحاب جواز الصغائر
rows.claim: Those who allow minor sins for prophets take the burden as a minor sin; its description as breaking the back reflects the Prophet's intense grief and remorse despite forgiveness.
rows.anchor: الذين يجوزون الصغائر على الأنبياء عليهم السلام حملوا هذه الآية عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second defense of the minor-sin reading is that the sin greatly affected the reward that would be lost through it, justifying the description of its weight.
rows.anchor: وصفه بذلك لأن تأثيره فيما يزول به من الثواب عظيم

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Rāzī objects that the minor-sin defense conflicts with the Qāḍī's view that God must forgive minor sins: this verse presents forgiveness as a favor, which cannot be gratitude for an obligation.
rows.anchor: أن العفو عن الصغيرة واجب على الله تعالى عند القاضي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the burden was sins the Prophet had committed in the pre-prophetic Jāhiliyya, which weighed on him and were forgiven.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : كانت للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another non-sin reading is the heavy duties of prophethood: managing its charge and preserving its requirements and rights, which God made easy for him.
rows.anchor: أن المراد منه تخفيف أعباء النبوة التي تثقل الظهر من القيام بأمرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden can mean distress at people changing Abraham's religion while the Prophet lacked power to stop them, until God strengthened him and commanded him to follow Abraham's way.
rows.anchor: الوزر ما كان يكرهه من تغييرهم لسنة الخليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be the sins of the Prophet's community, which weighed on him as he wondered what he could do for them; God assured him He would not punish them while he was among them and promised intercession later.
rows.anchor: ذنوب أمته صارت كالوزر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is that God protected the Prophet from a burden that would break his back if he had sinned; “setting down” is a metaphor for infallibility, illustrated by a report that God put him to sleep at a pre-prophetic wedding.
rows.anchor: عصمناك عن الوزر الذي ينقض ظهرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the illustrative report, the Prophet attended a wedding with drums and pipes before his mission, but God made him sleep until the next day's heat woke him.
rows.anchor: ما روي أنه حضر وليمة فيها دف ومزامير قبل البعثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may mean the awe and fear at the first meeting with Gabriel, when the Prophet trembled and nearly cast himself from a mountain, later becoming familiar and longing for Gabriel.
rows.anchor: الوزر ما أصابه من الهيبة والفزع في أول ملاقاة جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be the abuse and insults that nearly broke the Prophet and made him tremble; God strengthened him until he could endure a bloodied face and pray for his people's guidance.
rows.anchor: الوزر ما كان يلحقه من الأذى والشتم حتى كاد ينقض ظهره

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the account of enduring abuse, the Prophet said “God, guide my people,” when they had bloodied his face.
rows.anchor: ثم قواه الله تعالى حتى صار بحيث كانوا يدمون وجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the sūra came after Abū Ṭālib and Khadīja died, the burden was grief at losing them; God lifted it by raising the Prophet to heaven, where angels greeted him and his renown was raised.
rows.anchor: لئن كان نزول السورة بعد موت أبي طالب وخديجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be the bewilderment before prophethood: the Prophet's reason made him feel overwhelmed by God's unrepayable blessings because he did not know how to serve God; revelation and duty taught him how to obey and relieved that shame.
rows.anchor: أن المراد من الوزر والثقل الحيرة التي كانت له قبل البعثة
